title: 2 Chronicles 32:1–8
context: After these things and this faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria invades Judah, a crisis also told in 2 Kings 18–19 and Isaiah 36–37, each with its own emphasis and details. Chronicles alone reports Hezekiah’s counsel with his princes to stop the springs outside the city, his repair of the walls, the strengthening of the Millo, and the making of weapons, and his speech urging the people to be strong and courageous because there is a greater one with them than with the Assyrian king. The account in Chronicles does not mention the tribute Hezekiah paid in 2 Kings 18:14–16. Hezekiah’s work on the waters is mentioned again in 32:30 and in 2 Kings 20:20, and many connect it with the tunnel known today as Hezekiah’s or the Siloam tunnel, though such identifications should be stated with caution. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat the passage as shared ground about wise preparation joined with trust that the LORD fights for his people.

verses.text: After these things and this faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came, entered into Judah, encamped against the fortified cities, and intended to win them for himself.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Sennacherib invading Judah after these things and this faithfulness. Faithfulness does not exempt God’s people from trials.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the timing as a test that will display God’s power to deliver (compare 2 Kings 18:13; Isaiah 36:1). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober reminder that trials can follow obedience.

verses.text: When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come, and that he was planning to fight against Jerusalem,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah recognizing that Sennacherib intends to fight against Jerusalem. He assesses the danger clearly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his awareness as the beginning of wise and faithful response. Both traditions commonly read the verse as realism that prepares for action.

verses.text: he took counsel with his princes and his mighty men to stop the waters of the springs which were outside of the city, and they helped him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah taking counsel with his leaders to stop the springs outside the city. Faith and practical planning go together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see wise preparation as consistent with trust in God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as using ordinary means responsibly.

verses.text: Then many people gathered together and they stopped all the springs and the brook that flowed through the middle of the land, saying, “Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find abundant water?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see many people stopping the springs and the brook so that the Assyrians would not find water. The community works together in defense.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the shared effort as wise stewardship in crisis. Both traditions commonly read the verse as practical action alongside faith, holding historical identifications with caution.

verses.text: He took courage, built up all the wall that was broken down, and raised it up to the towers, with the other wall outside, and strengthened Millo in David’s city, and made weapons and shields in abundance.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah repairing the walls, strengthening the Millo, and making weapons and shields. Preparation is thorough.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his diligence as responsible leadership under God. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that trust in God does not exclude preparation.

verses.text: He set captains of war over the people, gathered them together to him in the wide place at the gate of the city, and spoke encouragingly to them, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah setting captains over the people and speaking encouragingly to them at the city gate. Leaders strengthen the courage of others.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his words as pastoral leadership in a time of fear. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a model of encouragement under pressure.

verses.text: “Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid or dismayed because of the king of Assyria, nor for all the multitude who is with him; for there is a greater one with us than with him.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah urging the people to be strong and courageous, for there is a greater one with them. Faith looks beyond visible odds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assurance as echoing God’s promises of presence (compare Deuteronomy 31:6; 2 Kings 6:16). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to trust God’s presence (compare 1 John 4:4).

verses.text: An arm of flesh is with him, but the LORD our God is with us to help us and to fight our battles.” The people rested themselves on the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Hezekiah contrasting the arm of flesh with the LORD who fights for his people, and the people resting on his words. Trust brings rest.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the contrast as central to biblical faith (compare Jeremiah 17:5; Psalm 20:7). Both traditions commonly read the verse as shared ground about trusting God rather than human strength.
